# What Changes On-Prem: SaaS, Customer-Managed, Air-Gapped and Hybrid

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against RFC 5280, RFC 9525 and local OpenSSL 3.6.2 runs. The deployment-model names are industry vocabulary, not a standard (see Sources).

Builds on: networking basics (lesson network-protocols); containers and Kubernetes (lesson containers-ci/03-kubernetes-for-a-service-engineer)

Scope: general concepts about shipping software that runs in a customer's environment. This lesson says nothing about how any particular company packages, supports or bills its on-prem offering. In week 1, replace the generic nouns below with the real ones.

## The problem and why it matters

In SaaS you run the software. You own the hardware choices, the deploy button, the dashboards, and the shell. When something breaks you log in, look, patch and ship, often within the hour.

On-prem (a customer runs it in their data center or their own cloud account) flips almost all of that. The customer owns the machines, the network and the schedule. You own the code and the promise it works. A data plane engineer who only knows SaaS will design things that quietly assume access they no longer have: "just exec into the pod" (open a shell inside a running container; a pod is Kubernetes' unit of running containers), "just hit the vendor API", "just ship a fix tonight".

Interviewers ask about this because it separates people who have only operated their own service from people who can ship a product another team operates. Fast iteration meets slow, careful change windows.

## First principles

1. **Who holds the keys decides what you can do.** The question to ask of any design is: who has shell, who has credentials, who can deploy. On-prem the answers are "the customer" for all three.
2. **Split by trust and data, not by convenience.** A *control plane* decides what should happen (configuration, scheduling, users). A *data plane* does the work on customer data. The data plane is what customers insist stays inside their walls.
3. **Connections are initiated from the inside.** Customer firewalls (network filters that decide which connections may pass) are the customer's to configure, and opening a path from the outside in needs their approval, which many will not give. A system that needs the vendor to dial in will often be blocked.
4. **You cannot assume uniformity.** Different kernels (the core of the operating system), GPUs, storage classes (the disk types the cluster offers), proxies, certificate authorities (CAs, the bodies whose signatures your TLS connections trust). Everything you do not pin down becomes a support ticket.
5. **Every fix has a long tail.** A SaaS fix reaches everyone at once. An on-prem fix reaches each customer when they choose to upgrade, so old versions stay alive for a long time and you must support several at once.

## How it works

### The deployment spectrum

```
 who runs the software, left to right
 SaaS        Hybrid       Customer-    Air-gapped
                          managed
 ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐
 │control │ │control │ │control │ │control │
 │ vendor │ │ vendor │ │customer│ │customer│
 ├────────┤ ├────────┤ ├────────┤ ├────────┤
 │ data   │ │ data   │ │ data   │ │ data   │
 │ vendor │ │customer│ │customer│ │customer│
 ├────────┤ ├────────┤ ├────────┤ ├────────┤
 │network │ │ mixed  │ │ their  │ │ no link│
 │ yours  │ │        │ │ network│ │ outside│
 └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘
```

Read each column as "who operates this layer". *Hybrid* is the popular middle: the vendor keeps the easy-to-update control plane, and the customer runs the data plane next to their data. *Air-gapped* means no network path to the outside at all, so updates arrive on physical media or through a one-way transfer process, and nothing phones home.

### Hybrid connectivity: dial out, never in

```
  customer environment            vendor cloud
 ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐
 │  data plane         │        │ control plane│
 │ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ │ HTTPS  │  config      │
 │ │worker │ │ agent ├─┼──out──▶│  scheduling  │
 │ └───┬───┘ └───────┘ │        │  UI / API    │
 │     │               │◀─ reply│              │
 │ ┌───┴────┐          │ (same  └──────────────┘
 │ │ their  │          │  conn)
 │ │ data   │  no inbound
 │ └────────┘  allowed
 └─────────────────────┘
```

The agent (a small program that runs next to the data and talks to the vendor) opens a long-lived outbound connection (or polls, asking repeatedly "any new work?") and pulls work and config down. The control plane never opens a connection into the customer. Two consequences you must design for:

- **Latency and loss.** The link can drop for hours. The data plane must keep running on its last known config and queue its status for later.
- **Proxies.** Outbound traffic often goes through an HTTP(S) proxy (a middleman server all web traffic must pass through) that may inspect TLS (the encryption layer behind HTTPS) using the customer's own certificate authority. Your agent needs proxy settings and a way to trust a custom CA (lesson 05).

### What you lose and what the customer gains

| You lose | Why it hurts |
|---|---|
| Shell and debugger access | Every debugging step must be something the customer can run or send you |
| Uniform hardware | Bugs appear only on one GPU model or kernel |
| Fast fixes | A patch needs a release, a customer change window and an upgrade |
| Free telemetry | Telemetry (metrics and logs) stays inside the customer unless they choose to send them |

| The customer gains | Why they pay for it |
|---|---|
| Data residency | Data stays in a chosen country or facility |
| Compliance | Auditors can inspect the environment and the controls |
| Control over change | Upgrades happen on their schedule |
| Use of existing infrastructure | Their GPUs, their network, their identity provider |

### The support-engineer model

Because you cannot log in, a human on the customer side becomes your hands. Typical flow: customer reports a symptom, support asks for a *support bundle* and runs a prescribed diagnostic command, engineering reads the bundle and proposes a change, the customer applies it. The quality of the diagnostics you built in advance decides how long that loop takes. Lesson 04 covers this in depth.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** a hybrid customer's new workers show as "never connected" in the control plane. The install finished with no errors.

1. **Is the data plane actually running?** Ask for pod or service status and the agent log. If it is crash-looping (starting, dying and restarting in a loop), this is not a connectivity problem.
2. **Does the agent log show connection attempts?** If it logs "connection timed out", traffic is being dropped. If it logs "certificate verify failed", the network works and trust does not.
3. **Is there a proxy?** Ask whether the customer's outbound traffic must use one. An agent with no proxy configuration times out against a firewall that only allows the proxy.
4. **Is TLS being intercepted?** A proxy that re-signs traffic with the customer's CA breaks the agent unless the agent trusts that CA.
5. **Does the destination match an allow-list?** (A list of the only destinations the firewall permits.) Many customers allow only specific hostnames or IP ranges outbound. Share the exact hostnames and ports you need, and note that a hostname allow-list breaks if you add a new endpoint later without telling them.
6. **Is the clock right?** Certificate validation fails if the host's clock is far off.

**Fix:** depends on the branch. Typical: set the proxy variables and mount the customer CA bundle into the agent, then have the customer add your hostnames to the allow-list. The durable fix is shipping a built-in connectivity check (`diagnose connectivity`) that tests DNS (name to address lookup), TCP (the connection itself), TLS and auth separately and prints which layer failed, so the next customer finds this in a minute.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| Customer data cannot leave their boundary (regulation, contract, sensitivity) | You can win the customer with SaaS; on-prem multiplies your support cost |
| Customer already owns GPUs or capacity they want to reuse | You cannot afford a support organization and diagnostic tooling |
| Hybrid: you want fast control-plane iteration with data kept local | The data plane needs frequent changes that customers will not accept quickly |
| Air-gapped: the customer's environment forbids any external link | You depend on vendor-hosted services at runtime (model downloads, license servers) |

## Interview questions

1. What is the difference between SaaS, hybrid, customer-managed and air-gapped? *Probe:* which one do customers with strict data rules usually want first, and why? *Outline:* who runs the control plane, who runs the data plane, whether any external network path exists.
2. Why do hybrid designs usually use outbound-only connections? *Probe:* what do you do when the link is down for a day? *Outline:* inbound firewall rules; agent pulls work; data plane continues with last known config and buffers status.
3. What do you lose when you can no longer log in? How do you compensate? *Outline:* build support bundles, structured logs, health endpoints and a diagnostic command before you need them.
4. A customer on version N-3 reports a bug fixed two releases ago. What do you do? *Probe:* how do you decide how many versions to support? *Outline:* have a support policy; backport only severe issues; show them the upgrade path; this is why compatibility matters (lesson 03).
5. How would you design the agent that connects a customer data plane to a vendor control plane? *Outline:* outbound HTTPS, proxy support, custom CA support, reconnect with backoff (wait longer after each failed try), local operation while disconnected, versioned protocol.
6. What is an air-gapped install and what must you ship differently? *Outline:* all images, charts, dependencies, license material and docs travel as a bundle; no runtime downloads, no phone-home.

**Worked exercise:** draw the hybrid diagram from memory. Mark which side owns configuration, which owns data, which direction every connection is opened, and what keeps working when the link drops.

## Checklist

1. I can name the four deployment models and say who runs each layer.
2. I can explain control plane vs data plane and why data stays local.
3. I can explain why connections are outbound-only and what proxies change.
4. I can list what I lose on-prem and what the customer gains.
5. I can walk a "never connected" report through DNS, TCP, TLS, proxy and allow-list checks.

## Common wrong answers

- "Just give us SSH or VPN access." Many customers will refuse, and some contracts or rules forbid it.
- "On-prem is SaaS in a different place." The difference is operator, access and upgrade cadence, not location.
- "We will fix it and redeploy tonight." Not without the customer's change window.
- "Phone-home telemetry is fine." Not by default; it may violate contracts or air-gap rules.

## Sources

Checked:
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280 (section 4.1.2.5): a certificate's validity period runs from notBefore through notAfter, which is why a badly wrong host clock breaks certificate validation. Local check: `openssl x509 -checkend` on a throwaway 5-day certificate reported "will expire" for 10 days and "will not expire" for 1 day (OpenSSL 3.6.2).
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9525.html: clients match DNS names against the `subjectAltName` extension, not the Common Name.
- The control-plane/data-plane split, the dial-out agent pattern, proxies and allow-lists are design reasoning, not documented tool behaviour. They are stated as "often" or "many customers", not as universal facts.

The deployment-model definitions here are common industry vocabulary, not a standard; vendors use these words differently, so confirm the real definitions in week 1. Not checked: any vendor-specific behavior, firewall products.
